vignette: A 32-year-old woman is typed before surgery. Forward typing shows agglutination with anti-A and anti-B; reverse typing shows agglutination with A1 cells and B cells. The screen is negative.
stem: Which of the following is the most likely explanation?

choices.text: A forward/reverse ABO discrepancy is present
The patient has a cold autoantibody

explanation: Forward typing suggests group AB (A and B antigens present) but reverse typing shows both anti-A and anti-B in the plasma, which contradicts group AB. This is a classic forward/reverse ABO discrepancy that must be resolved — by repeat testing, extended panel, and history (recent transfusion, stem cell transplant, or subgroups) — before any blood is issued.

rationales.A: Group AB plasma contains neither anti-A nor anti-B, so reverse typing should show no agglutination with A1 or B cells — but it does.
rationales.B: Group O red cells react with neither anti-A nor anti-B in forward typing — but this patient's cells reacted with both.
rationales.C: Correct: forward and reverse results disagree, which by definition is an ABO discrepancy requiring resolution before transfusion.
rationales.D: A cold autoantibody would typically pan-agglutinate in the screen and controls; the antibody screen here is negative.

misconception: Students often pick A because they read only the forward typing and forget that reverse typing must agree.
reference: Harmening's Blood Banking and Transfusion Fundamentals, 6th ed., Ch. 3
examTraps: Always interpret forward and reverse typing together; disagreement is a discrepancy, not a blood type.

vignette: A newborn requires an emergency red cell transfusion. Reverse typing has not been performed yet.
stem: Why is reverse (serum) typing unreliable in newborns?

choices.text: Newborn red cells lack A and B antigens
Newborn plasma antibodies are weak or absent, and any present are often maternal IgG
Newborn samples clot too quickly for reverse typing

explanation: ABO antigens are present at birth (though weaker than in adults), but isohemagglutinins are not reliably produced until several months of age; any antibody detected may be passively transferred maternal IgG. Reverse typing is therefore unreliable, and forward typing plus history guides newborn transfusion (usually group O, antigen-negative components).

rationales.A: A and B antigens are expressed on newborn red cells, just at reduced strength compared with adults.
rationales.B: Correct: isohemagglutinin production is immature in newborns, and detected antibody may be maternal, so reverse typing cannot be trusted.
rationales.C: Anti-D only exists in RhD-negative individuals who were sensitized; this is irrelevant to ABO reverse typing.
rationales.D: Sample handling is the same as for adult specimens; clotting is not the reason reverse typing is unreliable.

misconception: Students often think newborns lack ABO antigens entirely; they lack reliable antibodies, not antigens.
reference: Harmening's Blood Banking and Transfusion Fundamentals, 6th ed., Ch. 3
examTraps: Antigens are present at birth; antibodies are not reliable — the reverse of the usual adult logic.

vignette: A group O patient with anti-A and anti-B in the plasma needs platelet transfusion.
stem: Which statement about group O plasma is correct?

choices.text: Group O plasma is the universal plasma donor
Group O red cells are the universal red cell donor because they lack A and B antigens
Group O individuals lack the H antigen
Group O plasma can safely be given to group A recipients in unlimited volumes

explanation: Group O red cells carry neither A nor B antigen, so they can be given to recipients of any ABO group (universal red cell donor). Group O plasma, however, contains anti-A and anti-B and is the LEAST suitable plasma for non-group-O recipients — it is high-titer plasma that can cause hemolysis.

rationales.A: Wrong: group AB is the universal plasma donor; group O plasma contains anti-A and anti-B.
rationales.B: Correct: absence of A and B antigens on group O red cells makes them the universal red cell donor.
rationales.C: Group O individuals have abundant unmodified H antigen (the O allele makes a non-functional transferase).
rationales.D: Group O plasma contains anti-A that can hemolyze group A recipient red cells, especially in platelet or plasma transfusion.

misconception: Students often flip the universal donor concepts: universal RBC donor is group O, universal plasma donor is group AB.
reference: Harmening's Blood Banking and Transfusion Fundamentals, 6th ed., Ch. 2
examTraps: 'Universal donor' depends on the component: O for red cells, AB for plasma.
